clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive leukoencephalopathy caused by variants in any of the five subunits of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2B (EIF2B1 to EIF2B5)

The defining clinical feature is episodic, stepwise deterioration provoked by stressors such as febrile illness, minor head trauma or acute fright, sometimes with disproportionate decline or coma followed by partial recovery
The adult-onset form is generally milder and more slowly progressive than the infantile disease, with spasticity, cerebellar ataxia and cognitive or behavioural change predominating
Affected women may have primary or secondary ovarian failure, giving the ovarioleukodystrophy phenotype, which is an important clue in females

The MRI hallmark is diffuse white matter rarefaction and cystic degeneration, so that over time the abnormal white matter takes on a signal close to cerebrospinal fluid on all sequences, sometimes with a radiating stripe pattern within it
Diagnosis rests on the characteristic imaging together with the stress-sensitive clinical course, confirmed by EIF2B gene testing
There is no specific therapy; management is supportive and includes avoiding and promptly treating triggers such as fever and head injury
reference.pathophysiology: Vanishing white matter disease is caused by biallelic variants in genes encoding subunits of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2B (eIF2B), a guanine nucleotide exchange factor central to the initiation of protein synthesis and to the integrated stress response. Impaired eIF2B activity dysregulates the cellular response to stress, rendering glial cells, particularly astrocytes and oligodendrocytes, abnormally vulnerable. Physiological stressors such as fever, trauma or fright overwhelm this defective stress response, precipitating white matter injury. Progressive loss and cystic breakdown of the white matter produce the characteristic rarefaction in which affected tissue comes to resemble cerebrospinal fluid on imaging.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple sclerosis and other inflammatory demyelination
Other adult-onset genetic leukoencephalopathies (including LBSL and adult Alexander disease)
CADASIL and other hereditary small-vessel diseases
Premature ovarian insufficiency with an unrelated incidental white matter change
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to demonstrate diffuse white matter rarefaction with cystic change and a CSF-like signal, and any radiating stripe pattern
EIF2B1 to EIF2B5 sequencing or gene panel to confirm the diagnosis
Endocrine assessment of ovarian function in affected women
Neuropsychological evaluation to characterise cognitive involvement
Exclusion of inflammatory and infective causes (CSF, oligoclonal bands) where multiple sclerosis is considered
Serial imaging to document the evolving white matter rarefaction
redFlags: Rapid deterioration or coma following fever, head trauma or acute fright
New encephalopathy in a patient with known disease requiring assessment for a treatable trigger
Progressive cognitive decline with loss of independence
Dysphagia and aspiration risk as the disease advances
reference.prognosis: Adult-onset vanishing white matter disease is usually slower and milder than childhood forms, but remains progressive and is punctuated by stress-related episodes of decline that may not fully reverse; the overall course varies widely with genotype and age at onset. Careful avoidance of triggers can reduce episodic deterioration, though cumulative disability tends to accrue over time.
pitfalls: Not recognising the stress-provoked, stepwise course as a specific clue to the diagnosis
Misinterpreting the CSF-like white matter as atrophy or old ischaemia rather than rarefaction
Overlooking ovarian failure in women, which points towards the diagnosis
Mislabelling the disorder as multiple sclerosis and giving inappropriate immunotherapy
Failing to advise patients and families about avoiding and promptly managing fever and head injury
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
